easy.text: Kievan Rus, a medieval East Slavic state considered an ancestor of modern Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus, was centered on which city?

options.feedback: Correct -- Kyiv served as the political and cultural center of Kievan Rus for centuries.
Moscow rose to prominence much later, after Kievan Rus had declined -- Kyiv was the earlier state's center.
Novgorod was an important early trading city, but the state itself is named for and centered on Kyiv.
St. Petersburg was founded centuries later, in the 18th century, long after Kievan Rus.

medium.text: Kievan Rus's ruling dynasty is traditionally traced to Rurik, a leader of which seafaring people, said to have been invited to rule by local Slavic tribes?

options.feedback: Correct -- tradition holds that Rurik and his fellow Varangians were invited from Scandinavia to bring order to the region.
The Mongols invaded Kievan Rus centuries later -- Rurik's dynasty traces to the earlier Varangians.
The Ottomans emerged centuries later in Anatolia, unrelated to Rurik's founding dynasty.
The Huns were active many centuries earlier, unrelated to Rurik's Varangian origins.

hard.text: Grand Prince Vladimir the Great's decision in 988 CE to adopt which religion from the Byzantine Empire profoundly shaped the future religious identity of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus?

options.feedback: Correct -- Vladimir's baptism and adoption of Byzantine Orthodox Christianity set the religious course for the region for centuries.
Vladimir's choice connected Kievan Rus to Byzantine Orthodoxy, not the Roman Catholic Church of Western Europe.
According to tradition Vladimir considered several faiths, but he ultimately chose Byzantine Orthodox Christianity, not Islam.
Tradition holds Vladimir also considered Judaism, but his final choice was Byzantine Orthodox Christianity.

easy.easy: This city sits on the Dnieper River and is now the capital of Ukraine.
easy.medium: This city gives its name to the medieval state that predates Moscow's rise to power.
easy.hard: This city, not Moscow or the much-later St. Petersburg, anchored the medieval East Slavic state that later split into several modern nations.

medium.easy: These seafaring warriors and traders came originally from Scandinavia.
medium.medium: This group is linked to Viking activity in Northern and Eastern Europe.
medium.hard: This Scandinavian-linked group, distinct from later Mongol invaders, the Ottomans, or the much earlier Huns, is credited with founding the ruling dynasty of Kievan Rus.

hard.easy: This faith is centered on Byzantine tradition, distinct from Western Christianity.
hard.medium: This religion connected Kievan Rus culturally and spiritually to Constantinople.
hard.hard: This branch of Christianity, distinct from Western Catholicism and from other faiths Vladimir is said to have weighed, became the lasting religious identity of the region after 988 CE.

easy.text: The Investiture Controversy was a major medieval conflict between the Papacy and secular rulers over the authority to appoint whom?

options.feedback: Correct -- the dispute centered on whether popes or secular rulers had the right to appoint church officials like bishops.
The controversy concerned religious appointments, not military command positions.
Tax administration was not the issue at stake -- the dispute was over appointing church officials.
Universities as we know them did not yet exist in this form -- the dispute concerned church appointments.

medium.text: The Investiture Controversy's most dramatic early episode saw Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV do what outside the castle of Canossa to seek the pope's forgiveness?

options.text: Stand as a barefoot penitent in the snow for days to lift his excommunication
options.feedback: Correct -- Henry IV's public penance at Canossa in 1077 became a famous symbol of the struggle between imperial and papal power.

options.text: Sign a formal treaty ceding all his lands to the pope
options.feedback: Henry sought forgiveness through humble penance, not by formally surrendering his territories.

options.text: Wage a symbolic battle with the pope's guards
options.feedback: There was no symbolic battle -- Henry's approach was one of humble, public penance.

options.text: Offer his crown to the Byzantine emperor
options.feedback: Byzantium played no role in this episode -- Henry sought reconciliation directly with the pope.

hard.text: The Investiture Controversy was formally resolved in 1122 by which agreement, which split the appointment process between spiritual and secular authority?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Concordat of Worms distinguished spiritual investiture (by the church) from secular investiture (by the emperor).
The Peace of Westphalia ended a much later conflict, in 1648, unrelated to the Investiture Controversy's resolution.
The Treaty of Verdun in 843 divided Charlemagne's empire, centuries before the Investiture Controversy was resolved.
The 1521 Diet of Worms addressed Martin Luther and the Reformation, centuries after the Investiture Controversy ended.

easy.easy: This authority concerned appointing clergy specifically, not military, tax, or academic positions, which is what set the pope and secular rulers at odds.
easy.medium: This dispute was about who -- the church or secular rulers -- got to select bishops.
easy.hard: This authority involves choosing religious leaders for church positions.

medium.easy: This act, a barefoot public penance in the snow, was Henry IV's way of seeking to lift his excommunication -- not a treaty, a battle, or an appeal to Byzantium.
medium.medium: This act was a plea for forgiveness, performed outside a fortress in Italy.
medium.hard: This act involved humility and endurance in harsh winter conditions.

hard.easy: This agreement, from the early 12th century and distinct from a 17th-century peace, a 9th-century territorial division, and a 16th-century religious hearing, finally resolved the investiture dispute.
hard.medium: This agreement split appointment authority between church and emperor in the early 1100s.
hard.hard: This agreement's name refers to a German city.

easy.text: In 1453, which empire's forces captured Constantinople, ending the nearly 1,000-year-old Byzantine Empire?

options.feedback: Correct -- Ottoman forces conquered Constantinople in 1453, bringing the Byzantine Empire to an end.
The Mongols were active centuries earlier and were not the force that captured Constantinople in 1453.
The Persian Empire of this era was not the conquering force -- that was the Ottoman Empire.
The Holy Roman Empire was a separate Western European power, not the force that took Constantinople.

medium.text: Which Ottoman sultan led the successful 1453 siege that captured Constantinople?

options.feedback: Correct -- Mehmed II, later known as 'the Conqueror,' led the siege that finally took Constantinople.
Suleiman ruled decades later, at the height of Ottoman power -- Mehmed II led the 1453 conquest.
Osman I founded the Ottoman dynasty over a century earlier and did not lead the 1453 siege.
Selim I ruled in the early 16th century, after Mehmed II's conquest of Constantinople.

hard.text: Constantinople's formidable land fortifications, the Theodosian Walls, had withstood sieges for centuries. What new military technology finally allowed the Ottomans to breach them in 1453?

options.feedback: Correct -- enormous bombards, including ones built by a Hungarian engineer named Orban, pounded holes in walls that had held for a thousand years.
Siege towers were an older technology -- the decisive new factor in 1453 was massive gunpowder artillery.
Greek fire was actually a Byzantine weapon used against attackers in earlier centuries, not an Ottoman weapon that breached the walls in 1453.

options.text: A prolonged naval blockade alone, without any land assault
options.feedback: The Ottomans combined naval pressure with a land assault powered by massive cannon bombardment of the walls.

easy.easy: This empire was based in Anatolia and continued expanding for centuries after this conquest.
easy.medium: This empire's forces were led by a young sultan determined to capture the ancient Byzantine capital.
easy.hard: This empire, not the earlier Mongols, a separate Persian state, or the unrelated Holy Roman Empire, finally toppled the Byzantine capital in 1453.

medium.easy: This sultan earned the nickname 'the Conqueror' after this victory.
medium.medium: This sultan was young when he achieved what earlier sultans had failed to do.
medium.hard: This sultan, distinct from a later sultan famous for the empire's peak, an earlier dynasty founder, and another 16th-century ruler, personally led the 1453 siege.

hard.easy: This technology used gunpowder to launch heavy projectiles at fortifications.
hard.medium: This technology included giant cannons designed in part by a foreign engineer.
hard.hard: This technology marked a decisive leap in siege warfare, letting attackers batter down defenses that had resisted every prior method of assault.

easy.text: Which of the following are true about the Hanseatic League? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It was an alliance of merchant guilds and trading towns in Northern Europe
options.feedback: Correct -- the League united merchants and cities across Northern Europe for shared commercial advantage.

options.text: It dominated trade across the Baltic and North Seas
options.feedback: Correct -- the League's trade network was centered on these two northern European seas.

options.text: It was a Mediterranean naval empire ruled by a single king
options.feedback: The Hanseatic League was based in Northern Europe and was not ruled by a single monarch -- it was a commercial alliance of towns.

options.text: It was founded to spread a single new religion across Europe
options.feedback: The League's purpose was commercial, not religious -- it existed to protect and expand merchant trade interests.

medium.text: Which of the following are true about the Hanseatic League's structure and leadership? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The city of Lubeck is generally regarded as its leading and founding city
options.feedback: Correct -- Lubeck served as the League's most prominent city and unofficial leader.

options.text: It included dozens of allied towns spanning from the Netherlands to the Baltic region
options.feedback: Correct -- the League's membership grew to include a wide network of towns across Northern Europe.

options.text: It was governed by a single hereditary royal family
options.feedback: The League had no single ruling monarch -- it operated through cooperation among independent merchant towns.

options.text: It maintained a large standing army that conquered rival cities
options.feedback: The League relied on economic cooperation and shared privileges, not military conquest, to maintain its power.

hard.text: Which of the following accurately describe how the Hanseatic League maintained its economic power for centuries? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Through a network of trade agreements and shared commercial privileges among member towns
options.feedback: Correct -- cooperative trade agreements, not conquest, were the League's foundation of power.

options.text: By establishing trading posts (kontors) in foreign cities to secure favorable trading rights
options.feedback: Correct -- kontors in cities like Novgorod, Bergen, and London helped secure the League's commercial interests abroad.

options.text: By converting all member cities into a single centralized nation-state
options.feedback: Member towns remained politically independent -- the League never became a unified nation-state.

options.text: By receiving a religious mandate directly from the Pope granting exclusive trading rights
options.feedback: The League's authority came from commercial agreements among towns, not a papal religious mandate.

easy.easy: Both correct statements describe a commercial alliance of Northern European towns and its dominant seas, not a Mediterranean monarchy or a religious movement.
easy.medium: Both true statements involve merchant towns and two specific northern European bodies of water.
easy.hard: One correct answer is about who was in this alliance; the other is about which seas it dominated.

medium.easy: Both correct statements describe a specific leading city and a wide geographic network of independent towns, not a single royal family or a conquering military force.
medium.medium: Both true statements involve a specific German city's leadership role and a broad network of member towns.
medium.hard: One correct answer names its leading city; the other is about how widely its membership spread.

hard.easy: Both correct statements describe cooperative commercial arrangements and foreign trading posts, distinct from forming a single nation-state or claiming a religious mandate from the Pope.
hard.medium: Both true statements involve cooperative agreements and dedicated trading posts abroad, not conquest or centralization.
hard.hard: One correct answer is about shared trade deals; the other is about outposts in foreign cities.

easy.text: Joan of Arc, a young Frenchwoman who claimed to receive divine visions, is best known for leading French forces during which major medieval conflict?

options.feedback: Correct -- Joan of Arc rallied French troops during the long conflict between France and England known as the Hundred Years' War.
The Crusades were earlier religious wars fought over the Holy Land, not the conflict Joan of Arc fought in.
The Wars of the Roses were an English civil conflict fought after Joan of Arc's era, not the war she participated in.
The Reconquista took place on the Iberian Peninsula, a different conflict from the French-English war Joan of Arc fought in.

medium.text: Joan of Arc's most celebrated military achievement was lifting the siege of which French city in 1429?

options.feedback: Correct -- Joan's leadership helped break the English siege of Orleans, a turning point in the war.
Joan later took part in an unsuccessful assault on Paris, but her most famous victory was lifting the siege of Orleans.
Reims was where Joan helped bring about the coronation of Charles VII, not the site of the famous siege she lifted.
Rouen was the city where Joan was later tried and executed, not where she lifted a siege.

hard.text: Joan of Arc was ultimately captured, tried for heresy, and executed in 1431 in which city?

options.feedback: Correct -- Joan was tried by an English-backed church court and burned at the stake in Rouen in 1431.
Orleans was the site of her famous military victory, not her trial and execution.
Paris was the site of an unsuccessful assault Joan took part in, not her trial and execution.
Reims was the site of Charles VII's coronation, which Joan helped bring about, not her trial and execution.

easy.hard: This conflict, distinct from the earlier Crusades, a later English civil war, or the separate Iberian Reconquista, is the one Joan of Arc fought in.

hard.medium: This city held the court that condemned Joan for heresy.
hard.hard: This city, distinct from her military victory site, the site of an unsuccessful later assault, and the coronation city, is where Joan's trial and execution took place.

easy.text: The 1683 Ottoman siege of Vienna was ultimately broken by a relief force led by the king of which country?

options.feedback: Correct -- King Jan III Sobieski of Poland led the relief force that broke the siege of Vienna.
France did not lead the relief force -- that was led by the Polish king, Jan III Sobieski.
Russia was not the source of the relieving army -- Poland's king led the decisive relief force.
Spain played no role in relieving Vienna -- the relief force was led by the Polish king.

options.feedback: Correct -- after this defeat, the Ottoman Empire shifted from expansion to a long, gradual retreat from Central Europe.
The Byzantine Empire had already ended over two centuries earlier, in 1453 -- unrelated to this 1683 turning point.
The Holy Roman Empire, part of the defending coalition, continued on for over a century after this battle.
The Hanseatic League's decline stemmed from separate economic shifts, unrelated to the 1683 battle.

hard.text: The dramatic climax of the 1683 Battle of Vienna is often attributed to a massive cavalry charge carried out by which distinctive Polish cavalry force?

options.feedback: Correct -- the winged hussars' charge, led by Sobieski, is often described as one of the largest cavalry charges in history and helped break the siege.

The Teutonic Knights were a medieval military order from an earlier era, not the force credited with this 1683 charge.

easy.medium: This monarch's cavalry became legendary for its role in relieving the city.

easy.text: Marco Polo, a Venetian merchant traveler, journeyed across Asia in the 13th century to reach the court of which powerful ruler?

options.feedback: Correct -- Marco Polo traveled to the court of Kublai Khan, the Mongol ruler of Yuan Dynasty China.
Genghis Khan, Kublai's grandfather, had died decades before Marco Polo's journey -- it was Kublai Khan whose court Polo visited.

medium.text: Marco Polo's famous written account of his travels was dictated to a fellow writer while Polo was held where?

options.feedback: Correct -- Polo dictated his account to a writer named Rustichello da Pisa while both were imprisoned in Genoa.
Polo was not in a monastery when he dictated his account -- he was imprisoned in Genoa after a naval battle.
The written account was produced after Polo's return to Europe, while he was imprisoned, not while still at the Mongol court.

options.text: Aboard a ship en route home

hard.text: Marco Polo's account describes years of service in Kublai Khan's court, within a Mongol-led dynasty that ruled which country?

topic: the Mali Empire and Mansa Musa

easy.text: The Mali Empire's ruler Mansa Musa is famous in history for being considered what, largely due to his kingdom's vast gold resources?

options.text: Possibly the richest person in history
options.feedback: Correct -- Mansa Musa's immense wealth, built on West African gold and salt trade, has led many historians to call him the richest person in recorded history.

options.text: The first Muslim ruler in Africa
options.feedback: Muslim rulers existed in parts of Africa well before Mansa Musa -- his fame rests on his extraordinary wealth, not being the first.

options.text: The founder of the Songhai Empire

Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire in West Africa, entirely unrelated to Egypt's pharaohs.

medium.text: Mansa Musa's fame in the wider medieval world grew largely from his lavish pilgrimage in 1324 to which holy city?

options.feedback: Correct -- Mansa Musa's hajj to Mecca, accompanied by an enormous retinue and vast quantities of gold, became legendary.
Jerusalem was not the destination of Mansa Musa's famous pilgrimage -- his hajj was to Mecca.
Rome was not the destination of this pilgrimage -- Mansa Musa's journey was an Islamic hajj to Mecca.

options.feedback: Correct -- Mansa Musa's lavish gold spending while passing through Cairo reportedly devalued gold in the regional economy for years.
The economic disruption occurred in Cairo, along Mansa Musa's pilgrimage route, not in Baghdad.
Constantinople was not on Mansa Musa's hajj route -- the gold-driven economic disruption happened in Cairo.

easy.text: The Songhai Empire rose to become the dominant power in West Africa after the decline of which earlier empire?

options.feedback: Correct -- Moroccan forces armed with muskets and cannons overwhelmed Songhai's largely traditional army at the Battle of Tondibi.

topic: the Ethiopian Empire and the rock churches of Lalibela

options.feedback: Correct -- the Lalibela churches were monolithically carved out of volcanic rock, rather than built upward from stone blocks.

options.text: Assembled entirely from imported marble blocks
options.feedback: The churches were carved from the existing bedrock, not assembled from imported marble.

options.feedback: Correct -- Qutb-ud-din Aibak, once enslaved before rising through military ranks, founded the Delhi Sultanate's first dynasty.
Babur founded the later Mughal Empire, not the Delhi Sultanate's founding dynasty.
Akbar was a Mughal emperor, ruling centuries after the Delhi Sultanate's founding.
Timur famously raided Delhi but did not found the Delhi Sultanate's first dynasty.

hard.text: The Delhi Sultanate came to an end in 1526 when its last ruler was defeated at the Battle of Panipat by an invading Central Asian conqueror, who then founded which successor empire?

options.feedback: Correct -- Babur's victory at Panipat in 1526 ended the Delhi Sultanate and established the Mughal Empire.
The Maratha Empire rose later, challenging Mughal power -- it was not founded at the Battle of Panipat in 1526.
The Vijayanagara Empire was a separate southern Indian Hindu kingdom, not the empire founded after Panipat in 1526.
The Sur Empire briefly interrupted Mughal rule years later under Sher Shah Suri, but it was not the empire founded immediately after Panipat in 1526.

easy.easy: This subcontinent lies in South Asia.
easy.medium: This region is home to modern India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.
easy.hard: This subcontinent, distinct from Arabia, Southeast Asia, or Iberia, was the territory the Delhi Sultanate governed from its capital.

medium.easy: This founder's own dynasty is nicknamed after his personal background.
medium.medium: This founder rose from enslavement to found the Sultanate's very first ruling dynasty.
medium.hard: This founder, distinct from the later Mughal founder, a famous Mughal emperor, and an earlier Central Asian raider, established the Delhi Sultanate's first, 'Slave,' dynasty.

hard.easy: This empire became one of the most famous in Indian history, known later for grand architecture.
hard.medium: This empire was founded by the same conqueror who won the Battle of Panipat in 1526.
hard.hard: This empire, founded immediately after Panipat in 1526 and distinct from a later Hindu warrior confederacy, a southern Indian kingdom, or a later brief interrupting dynasty, succeeded the Delhi Sultanate.

easy.text: Which of the following were emperors of the Mughal Empire in India? (Select all that apply)

options.feedback: Correct -- Akbar was a major Mughal emperor known for expanding and consolidating the empire.
Correct -- Shah Jahan was a Mughal emperor, famous for commissioning the Taj Mahal.
Suleiman was an Ottoman sultan ruling from Constantinople, not a Mughal emperor in India.
Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire in West Africa, entirely unrelated to the Mughal Empire in India.

medium.text: Which of the following are true about the Mughal Empire's origins and rule? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It was founded in 1526 by Babur after defeating the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat
options.feedback: Correct -- Babur's victory at Panipat established Mughal rule in India.

options.text: It governed large parts of the Indian subcontinent for centuries
options.feedback: Correct -- Mughal rule endured, in various forms, from the 16th into the 19th century.

options.text: It was founded by Genghis Khan
options.feedback: Genghis Khan died centuries before the Mughal Empire was founded -- Babur, one of his distant descendants, founded it.

options.text: It was based primarily in Persia rather than India
options.feedback: The Mughal Empire was centered in the Indian subcontinent, not Persia, despite Persian cultural influence at its court.

hard.text: Which of the following accurately describe shifts in Mughal religious policy across different emperors' reigns? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Akbar pursued broad religious tolerance toward his non-Muslim subjects
options.feedback: Correct -- Akbar is known for policies promoting religious tolerance and dialogue among faiths.

options.text: Aurangzeb's later reign reintroduced more religiously conservative policies, including a reinstated tax on non-Muslims
options.feedback: Correct -- Aurangzeb reversed some of his predecessors' tolerant policies, straining relations with non-Muslim subjects.

options.text: Every Mughal emperor pursued identical religious policies with no change over time
options.feedback: Mughal religious policy shifted notably between rulers, especially between Akbar's tolerance and Aurangzeb's later conservatism.

options.text: The Mughal Empire had no interactions with or policies toward non-Muslim populations
options.feedback: Non-Muslim populations, especially Hindus, were central to Mughal governance and policy throughout the empire's history.

easy.easy: Both correct answers are Mughal emperors of India, distinct from an Ottoman sultan and a West African ruler entirely outside this empire.
easy.medium: Both true answers ruled the same Indian empire, one known for expansion and one for a famous tomb.
easy.hard: Both correct rulers governed from India, not the Middle East or West Africa.

medium.easy: Both correct statements describe the empire's 1526 founding by Babur after Panipat and its long rule over the Indian subcontinent, not a founder from centuries earlier or a Persian home base.
medium.medium: Both true statements involve a founding battle in 1526 and centuries of rule over India.
medium.hard: One correct answer is about how and when it began; the other is about how long it lasted.

hard.easy: Both correct statements describe a real documented shift -- from Akbar's tolerance to Aurangzeb's later conservatism -- not a claim of total uniformity or total disengagement from non-Muslim subjects.
hard.medium: Both true statements involve a documented shift in religious policy between two specific emperors' reigns.
hard.hard: One correct answer is about an emperor known for tolerance; the other is about a later emperor known for stricter policies.

easy.text: The Taj Mahal, one of the most famous buildings in the world, was built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a mausoleum for whom?

options.feedback: Correct -- Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth.
The Taj Mahal was built for Shah Jahan's wife, Mumtaz Mahal, not his mother.
Jahangir was Shah Jahan's father and predecessor as emperor, but the Taj Mahal was built for Shah Jahan's wife.

options.text: Himself, as his own planned tomb
options.feedback: Shah Jahan was later buried there alongside his wife, but the monument was originally built for Mumtaz Mahal.

medium.text: The Taj Mahal is located in which Indian city, which served as a Mughal capital?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Taj Mahal stands in Agra, a major Mughal capital city.
Delhi was another important Mughal capital, but the Taj Mahal itself is located in Agra.
Lahore was a significant Mughal city, but the Taj Mahal is located in Agra, not Lahore.
Jaipur is a well-known Indian city, but it was not built by the Mughals and does not house the Taj Mahal.

hard.text: The Taj Mahal's exterior is built primarily from which distinctive white stone, inlaid with semi-precious stones in a decorative technique?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Taj Mahal's gleaming white marble, inlaid with semi-precious stones (pietra dura), is one of its most celebrated features.
Red sandstone was used in other Mughal buildings like Fatehpur Sikri, but the Taj Mahal itself is famous for its white marble.
Limestone was not the defining material -- the Taj Mahal is renowned for its white marble construction.
Granite is not the material associated with the Taj Mahal's famous appearance -- that is white marble.

easy.easy: This person was the emperor's spouse, who died during childbirth.
easy.medium: This person's name is closely echoed in the monument's own name.
easy.hard: This person, not the emperor's mother, father, or the emperor himself, was the original intended occupant of this grand mausoleum.

medium.easy: This city sits along the Yamuna River in northern India.
medium.medium: This city, not the Mughal capital most associated with the Red Fort, is where the mausoleum was actually built.
medium.hard: This city, distinct from Delhi, Lahore, or Jaipur, was the specific Mughal capital chosen as the site for this famous tomb.

hard.easy: This material is prized for its bright white color.
hard.medium: This material is a fine, polished stone, not the reddish stone used at other Mughal sites.
hard.hard: This material, a luminous white stone inlaid with semi-precious gems, contrasts with the red sandstone used at other Mughal monuments like Fatehpur Sikri.

easy.text: The Ming Dynasty came to power in China in 1368 after overthrowing which foreign-led dynasty?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Ming Dynasty overthrew the Mongol-led Yuan Dynasty, restoring native Chinese rule.
The Qing Dynasty came after the Ming, not before it -- the Ming overthrew the earlier Yuan Dynasty.
The Tang Dynasty ruled centuries before the Ming and was not the dynasty it overthrew.
The Song Dynasty preceded the Yuan Dynasty and had already fallen to the Mongols before the Ming's rise.

medium.text: The Ming Dynasty is well known for a series of massive naval expeditions across the Indian Ocean, led by which admiral?

options.feedback: Correct -- Admiral Zheng He led enormous Ming treasure fleets on voyages as far as East Africa.
Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese explorer, not a Ming admiral.
Marco Polo was a Venetian traveler who visited the earlier Yuan Dynasty, not a Ming admiral.
Kublai Khan founded the earlier Yuan Dynasty and was not a Ming admiral.

hard.text: Much of the Great Wall of China as it exists and is visited today was largely rebuilt and reinforced with brick and stone during which dynasty's rule?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Ming Dynasty undertook massive reconstruction of the wall using brick and stone, producing much of what visitors see today.
The Qin Dynasty built early wall sections using mostly rammed earth, much of which has since eroded -- the durable version seen today is largely a Ming-era rebuild.
The Han Dynasty extended earlier wall sections, but the well-preserved brick-and-stone wall seen today is mainly a Ming-era achievement.
The Tang Dynasty is not associated with major Great Wall construction -- the well-known brick-and-stone version dates to the later Ming era.

easy.easy: This earlier dynasty was ruled by a Mongol imperial family, not ethnic Chinese rulers.
easy.medium: This earlier dynasty was founded by Kublai Khan, generations before the Ming rose to power.
easy.hard: This earlier dynasty, distinct from a later Chinese dynasty and from much earlier native Chinese dynasties, was overthrown to establish Ming rule.

medium.easy: This admiral commanded enormous 'treasure fleets' on long sea voyages.
medium.medium: This admiral's voyages reached as far as the coast of East Africa.
medium.hard: This admiral, distinct from a Portuguese explorer, a Venetian land traveler, and an earlier Mongol dynasty founder, led Ming China's famous naval expeditions.

hard.easy: This dynasty ruled centuries after the wall's very earliest sections were first built.
hard.medium: This dynasty rebuilt the wall using more durable materials than the earliest rammed-earth versions.
hard.hard: This dynasty, distinct from the wall's original earlier builders and from other dynasties not strongly associated with wall construction, gave the Great Wall much of its modern brick-and-stone form.
